speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) whether the recent digital banking disruptions by large local banks on 14 October 2023 are within MAS' expectations; (b) what has been the cost to consumers and business entities reliant on such banking services due to the recent disruptions; and (c) how will MAS ensure that consumers and business entities are given early warning of such service disruptions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) whether the Monetary Authority of Singapore (i) conducts regular inspections and off-site reviews of outsourced parties to handle critical IT and infrastructure systems for the domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs) and (ii) assesses the impact of outsourcing on the resilience of D-SIBs' IT infrastructure; and (b) if not, why.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) how does Singapore's penalty framework on digital banking disruptions committed by financial institutions compare with other large financial centers overseas; and (b) how effective have the penalties been in improving such service reliability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Prime Minister with the greater reliance on digital services for payment and other financial services and in light of the impact on consumers due to recent disruption of banking services, whether MAS will be requiring financial institutions and their service providers to take further measures to strengthen the resilience and reliability of their digital services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: asked the Prime Minister whether the Government has put in place minimum redundancy requirements and monitors concentration risk in the use of data centres by key local financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If Members are satisfied with the response, they may wish to withdraw their questions after my response.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: DBS and Citibank experienced system outages in the mid-afternoon of 14 October 2023, which affected their banking as well as their payment services.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These outages were caused by a malfunction of the cooling system in the data centre hosting both DBS' and Citibank's IT systems.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These IT systems support the delivery of retail and corporate banking services.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The temperature in the data centre rose above the optimal operating range, causing the banks' IT systems to shut down.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To restore the impacted services, DBS and Citibank immediately activated their IT disaster recovery and business continuity plans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: However, both banks encountered technical issues which prevented them from fully recovering their affected systems at their respective back-up data centres: DBS due to a network misconfiguration and Citibank due to connectivity issues.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Services at DBS and Citibank were progressively recovered from 8.21 pm and 7.05 pm respectively on 14 October, but only fully recovered in the early hours of 15 October.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The impact of the service outage was wide.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: DBS reopened its branches from 5.30 pm to 9.30 pm on 14 October to assist affected customers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Both banks provided updates via their social media platforms.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS requires banks to establish IT disaster recovery plans and to test these plans regularly.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Banks must conduct disaster recovery exercises with their back-up data centres to validate that critical systems and services can be restored within four hours of an outage.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The unscheduled downtime for a critical system affecting a bank's operations or service to customers must not exceed four hours within any 12-month period.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS does not oversee banks' external service providers, which are typically not financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is similar to the approach taken by regulators in other major jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The onus is on the banks to ensure that the external service providers they appoint to support their operations or service to customers, can meet MAS' requirements on operational resilience.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS also requires banks to maintain close oversight of the external service providers, so that they can deliver services with minimal disruptions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: DBS and Citibank have fallen short of MAS' requirements to ensure that their critical IT systems are resilient against prolonged disruptions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: While both banks conducted annual exercises to test the recovery of their IT systems at the back-up data centres, the specific issues that led to the delays in system recovery on 14 October did not surface during those tests.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will now elaborate on the accountability and remediation measures taken to uphold the reliability and recoverability of banking services.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Under the Banking Act, MAS can impose a fine of up to $100,000 on financial institutions found in breach of MAS' requirements on technology risk management.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With the passing of the Financial Services and Markets Act in 2022, which will progressively come into force next year, the fine quantum will be increased to a maximum of $1 million.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The fine quantum is consistent with existing local penalty regimes, such as those under the Telecommunications Act and the Personal Data Protection Act.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Besides fines, MAS uses a range of regulatory tools to address lapses in banks' risk management.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This includes additional capital requirements and suspension of specified businesses or activities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This translated to approximately S$1.6 billion in total additional regulatory capital at the time.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Holding additional regulatory capital comes with costs for the bank.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It increases the cost of capital and it is a key metric that drives business decisions such as dividends and investments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is a drag on the return on capital, which could in turn impact credit ratings as well as the stock price of the bank.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Banks are also accountable to their customers, but matters of compensation are better dealt with between the bank and its customers as it would be highly dependent on individual cases and circumstances.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS expects banks to have a fair process to deal with this.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS has instructed both DBS and Citibank to conduct thorough investigations into the root causes of the incidents that occurred on 14 October, as well as to put in place remediation measures to minimise future disruptions and outages and to strengthen their recoverability in the event of an outage.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In addition, the banks are required to provide to MAS, regular system availability reports relating to their critical systems.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS will also work with the financial industry to incorporate key learnings from these incidents into all banks' risk management controls, MAS' future technology risk supervisory approach as well as the next financial sector business continuity exercise, which is scheduled for 2024.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS has adopted a tougher stance against DBS because it experienced five disruptions to its banking services in the last eight months.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As directed by MAS, DBS convened a Special Board Committee earlier this year to oversee a full review of its IT resilience by an independent external expert.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There must not be any distractions that take away the needed resources and attention by the bank to strengthen its technology risk management systems and controls.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Another dimension of remediation has to do with data centres, which host the IT systems of not just the banks but also other critical sectors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government is studying ways to further strengthen the security and resilience of data centres, where lapses could result in a significant impact.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Contingency measures in the face of banking disruptions are key.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Disruptions can occur for a variety of reasons and can happen without warning.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: When they do occur, MAS expects banks to take prompt action to reduce inconvenience and costs to customers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This includes being proactive and transparent in updating affected customers on the status of service recovery and alternative services.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: While our banking system is generally robust, customers too must plan and prepare for contingencies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They can benefit from having alternative payment options and not be over-reliant on one provider for time-sensitive transactions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Indeed, during the recent service disruption, customers who were able to switch to alternative payment methods or providers or use cash as a last resort would have been less affected.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: While some disruption from time to time is unavoidable, we expect financial institutions to build and strengthen their capabilities to safely recover from any disruption within a reasonable time period.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Where financial institutions fail to do so, as with this incident, MAS will work with them to thoroughly investigate the incident, apply lessons learnt in our supervisory oversight of the financial industry and take necessary action to further strengthen the resilience of financial service delivery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I want to thank the Minister of State for reassuring us that there is a good plan laid out to strengthen our banking system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The first supplementary question is, over the last eight months as the Minister of State had pointed out, there were different parts of the digital banking system that has failed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Is the regulatory regime sufficiently tough enough of a deterrence to get the bank to focus its attention on strengthening the system?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because quite certainly, the non-essential items that were proposed, for example, merger and acquisitions (M&As) really depends on whether they have any in the pipeline.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If they do not, then this will be nothing short of a slap on the wrist.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How do these punishments compare to what we have in regimes overseas?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The second one is, through the course of the last eight months, there were various breakdowns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Certainly, DBS would have the system to warn consumers and users of the banking system, that there was a possible disruption and they should prepare for alternative ways of conducting business.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because many consumers were caught out – some of them were in restaurants, some of them were running their businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But they were not warned of these until they had to start to pay.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Nowadays, we get alerts quite frequently using the app or SMSes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Is this something the MAS will get DBS to consider?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First of all, I want to reiterate that: one, the banks have fallen short of MAS' requirements and expectations; two, that the outages and the length of time that are required to restore services are unacceptable; and three, the banks and the financial institutions involved are being held accountable.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, I mentioned earlier on that DBS is required to hold regulatory capital.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Members will know that this will be at great cost to the bank, as I had mentioned earlier on.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If you look at these as a whole, there is an impact on the banks in terms of regulatory capital that is costly to the bank – that is one.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Second, in the whole suite of measures, this is meant to allow for them to focus all of their attention into this – that they have the time, attention and resources to focus on this.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The third aspect of it, is to slow down the reduction of the number of ATMs and branches is also critical.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Because while we want to be digital-first, in our approach to digitalisation, we cannot be digital-only.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And therefore, all of these measures are, we think, at this point in time commensurate, but we will review them.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If the banks' response and mediation measures are not adequate, MAS will take further necessary actions to ensure that that is so.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: First, I would like to congratulate DBS for making record profit in the first half of this year, at more than $5 billion, which is a 45% rise compared to the same period in the previous year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, we note that DBS' IT and banking system has continued to have a lot of disruptions, despite the additional measures imposed by MAS, including the increase in capital requirement.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, that does not have a big impact on them.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I mentioned earlier on, the banks are and will be held accountable.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: DBS, on its own, also has acknowledged that the bank had fallen short of expectations and that senior management will be held accountable.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is in line with MAS' expectation for incentive structure, the bank's incentive structure to promote accountability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, all of these in concert is meant to send a very strong message that this is unacceptable and that we are holding banks accountable.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will look at what the banks have put in place during this period, how they are remediating, how they are fixing, how they are restoring this and, if necessary, we will have more – MAS will impose, potentially, more measures as necessary.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If I am unable to pay using one of the financial services providers, then I go to the other one; and if I lose confidence in one, I go to the other one.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I think number one, MAS will and is holding the banks accountable; two, the bank is holding itself accountable; and three, consumers can also hold the financial institutions accountable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I just have one clarification for Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He mentioned in his reply that the two banks had done their testing – they had the plans, they had done their testing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But despite the testing, which was done annually, these errors did still occur and these errors were impactful to users.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, is there a need to review the kind of testings and the requirements for the reporting of those testings, or further measures to be taken to ensure reliability?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I must thank the Minister of State for the earlier reply also, because I thought it was quite comprehensive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But it still requires the banks to adhere and also to ensure that the level of adherence is done.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think she raises a very important point.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, DBS' review; second, Citibank's review and then what MAS expects of all financial institutions, learning particularly from this incident, but also learning from the disruptions by financial institutions over the course of the last year or so.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, DBS' review, which was completed just a couple of months ago in 2023, has four pillars: first, technology risks, governance and oversight; second, incident management; third, how do you strengthen your system's resilience; and fourth, change management.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, DBS is undertaking this and they will look into this in detail.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But if you take a step back and look at the whole financial system as a whole, MAS expects all financial institutions to implement the adequate risk controls.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But Mr Speaker, Sir, if you allow me to just take one step back and to answer the Member's question also.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will accept that all forms of technology are not infallible.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: You see that happen in your smartphones; you see that in laptops; you also see that in your light bulbs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our approach to digitalisation is being digital first but not digital only.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Recently, when I had a dinner, I was unable to pay using my credit card that was not available to me.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: However, then I had to use my PayNow, for example.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, on a whole level, if you look at it, the service providers, the systems need to be accountable, they need to do their part.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We can make sure that we have contingency, the different ways to pay.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But, ultimately, I think it is important that in the age of digitalisation both financial institutions as well as consumers – have to be aware that some people may not be adept at technology.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And the banks and financial institutions and, in fact, companies, service providers must acknowledge that and must be able to provide other forms of payment approaches, so that others who are not so adept can still participate in the economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yip Chu Kang)
text: I note that MAS does not oversee external service providers like data centres.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yip Chu Kang)
text: But I am heartened to note that the Government will study strengthening the security of data centres.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yip Chu Kang)
text: My supplementary question is this: will MAS consider working with the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) and, perhaps, even the Cyber Security Agency (CSA) for a whole-of-Government approach to ensure that for data centres, there are build-in redundancy systems as well as robust plans to deter cyber attacks?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Please let me explain why MAS does not require banks to operate their own data centres.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Because not all banks possess the relevant expertise and the skills to do so.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Therefore, banks are given the option to tap on data centre operators' specialised know-how as well as the state-of-the-art data centre technologies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But, of course, as I mentioned earlier on, these things fail from time to time and, even if they have their exercises and their testing, some other parts of the system may fail.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And, therefore, the lessons learnt will be incorporated into reviews and as well as exercises.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To the Member's point about the whole-of-Government's approach to data centres, because it is not just confined to the financial services, the questions about the regulation of data centres have been addressed in response to Parliamentary Questions in this House.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Financial institutions are also expected to conduct due diligence and exercise adequate oversight of outsourced data centre service providers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These expectations are spelt out in MAS' Technology Risk Management Guidelines and Outsourcing Guidelines.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I see three more Members wanting to ask supplementary questions and I am conscious that Question Time is coming to an end.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, to all three, I will allow it and, likewise, for Minister of State Tan, if you can all keep your questions and your answers short.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For the consumers who were affected, the assurance that consumers would want is reliability of service.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: So, I do understand that Minister of State mentioned about a review that the MAS will be taking.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could we understand what will be the steps that MAS is looking into, to ensure that consumers' voices are heard in the review and that their assurance is actually reflected in the metrics of the review?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many average Singaporeans and small and medium enterprises (SMEs), especially the smaller merchants like hawkers do not have spare cash and maintain only one operating account with a particular Singaporean bank.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Neither do they have the means to seek legal recourse against the bank for the loss of business opportunities as well as the inconvenience caused.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, my question to MAS is, how does MAS decide when to impose a mortarium on new business venture or to impose a higher regulatory capital or to impose a larger network of ATMs?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I mentioned that earlier on with regard to how we are and must be digital first but not digital only.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, did you want to ask a question?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other supplementary questions for the Minister of State?
